b088: Who this is for: 5-HTP is not for every depressed person either. It could help, though, with a low-serotonin-looking pattern, where it's hard to fall asleep and your mood is low, without much warmth to it. At night you get anxious and keep going over the same things. It makes more sense if there's also a genetic or clinical reason to suspect a bottleneck in serotonin synthesis, like with Scott, whose genetic data pointed to a TPH2 bottleneck, and 5-HTP helped his sleep and mood. If you're already agitated or manic (it can push that further), on serotonergic meds, or using serotonergic psychedelics/entactogens (serotonin syndrome risk), you shouldn't be casually experimenting with it.
b090: Scott took 100 mg 5-HTP sublingually at night, with 10–20 mg P5P sublingually in the morning. The P5P isn't there as a stimulant, but as the active form of B6, which the enzyme that turns 5-HTP into serotonin (aromatic amino-acid decarboxylase) needs. Since he's slow-COMT and sensitive to too much P5P, the low dose matters, and it's one of those things where more isn't better.
b091: If you're sensitive, start lower and do the trial with 50 mg 5-HTP at night for 2–3 nights, then go up to 100 mg only if the lower amount is clearly helpful and isn't activating. You can also add 10–20 mg P5P in the morning, especially if the 5-HTP feels like it "almost works" but isn't converting cleanly. Don't do the trial at the same time as other changes (like UMP, agmatine, D-serine, psychedelics, or medication changes), since the point is to see whether the 5-HTP itself is doing anything. If it's the right tool, the first thing you'll usually notice is your sleep quality, the tone of your dreams, a warmer mood, or less rumination at night.
